newsitem.title: UK: BA shares take off on strike deal hopes.
newsitem.headline: BA shares take off on strike deal hopes.

text.p: Shares in British Airways Plc took off on Wednesday as investors hoped that a debilitating strike by the airline's cabin crew would be settled swiftly, analysts and traders said.

An 11 percent drop in the price of the shares since early June had also factored in the impact of the 72-hour strike, which started on Wednesday and grounded half its flights out of London, they said.
Shares ended 19-1/2p higher at 692-1/2p on modest volume of 2.2 million.
U.S. investors were also betting on a quick end to the industrial action. American Depository Receipts of British Airways traded 11/16 higher at $116-1/2 by 1550 GMT on the New York Stock Exchange.
"I think what happened is that the strike news got discounted before it happened," said Matthew Stainier, airlines analyst at Morgan Stanley.
"Once it happens, people are looking at what might happen next and the optimistic view is that it could end very quickly," he said.
Yet there was no real evidence on Wednesday to support hopes of a quick settlement in the dispute.
British Airways branded the strike illegal and said it was considering taking the union to court.
It also said it would not negotiate the terms of a deal to cut costs by 42 million pounds ($70.9 million), which provoked the dispute by the Transport and General Workers Union (T&G).

The airline, which declined to specify its losses from the strike, set a deadline of mid-afternoon for the union to respond to its charges that the action was illegal. BA said it would review its position if the union did not respond. The T&G made no immediate comment on BA's threat of legal action but officials said earlier the strike had strong backing.
"We have known for days there is going to be a strike," another analyst said. "I think we just have to wait and see what happens. It is a very difficult situation."

BA shares rose from the opening bell on Wednesday morning after a report in the Financial Times said "first signs of hope" had emerged of a resolution to the strike, with the union suggesting an arbiter could be called in.
A BA spokeswoman told Reuters it was hopeful of progress in the dispute but described as "inaccurate" the report of an arbiter being involved. ($ = 0.592 British Pounds)
